title: Register in the wild: yes, no-possession, and softening

grammarPoints.rule: Japanese has three yeses and three noes, and they split by AUDIENCE. Casual: うん / ううん. Neutral-polite: ええ. Formal: はい / いいえ. うん and ううん are one sound apart — the difference is a rising ん versus a falling one, so listen for the shape, not the letters.

antiPattern.why: うん to a teacher is too casual — はい or ええ

grammarPoints.rule: ううん and いいえ are one word in two registers: they answer no to a question. ちがう is not a third register of no — it is a different move. It CORRECTS: someone has said something wrong and you are telling them so. ちがう、ミカの ほんだ = 'no, it's Mika's book'. Politely it is ちがいます. Decline with いいえ; correct with ちがう.

examples.ja: ちがう、ミカの ほんだ。

grammarPoints.rule: はい does not always mean 'yes'. In conversation it is also AIZUCHI — the noise a listener makes to show they're still with you, like English 'mm-hm'. So はい can mean 'I'm listening', not 'I agree'. Watch what follows it: agreement continues the thought, aizuchi just keeps the speaker going.

ちょっと literally means 'a little', but its real job is SOFTENING. On its own — ちょっと… — it is a polite refusal that never says no. Japanese avoids flat rejection, so a trailing ちょっと is understood as 'that doesn't work for me'.

examples.ja: きょうは ちょっと。
examples.en: Today is… a bit difficult (trailing off = a polite no).

grammarPoints.rule: Two more words do the same softening work, and both lead the sentence without a particle. まあ hedges before you commit: まあ、いく is 'well… I'll go' — a yes with a shrug in it. よく is frequency: よく たべる is 'I eat it often'. After a verb of understanding it shades into 'well' — よく わかります, 'I understand it well'.

Turning something down has its own two words. だめ is the blunt one — 'no good', and by extension 'not allowed': それは だめ stops a friend mid-move. けっこう is the gentle refusal you hand a host or a shop assistant; it means 'I'm fine as I am, thank you', so ちゃは けっこうです declines the tea without ever saying no. だめ forbids, けっこう declines — they are not interchangeable.

Even 'I' carries register. わたし is the neutral one and is safe in any company. ぼく is casual and usually male — friends and family, never a first meeting with a teacher. Most of the time Japanese drops the subject altogether: いく on its own already means 'I'm going', so reach for a pronoun only when you need the contrast.

examples.ja: わたしは がくせいです。

grammarPoints.rule: しる is 'to know' — having a fact, a place or a person in your head. The form you will reach for constantly is its NEGATIVE: しりません to a teacher or a stranger, しらない to a friend, both 'I don't know'. Politeness lives in the tail, exactly as it does for every other verb: しります / しりません.

examples.ja: わたしは しりません。

antiPattern.ja: わたしは しるません。
antiPattern.why: ません attaches to the ます-stem, not the dictionary form — しる → しり + ません.

grammarPoints.rule: こちら is the polite こ-word. これ points at a thing and ここ at a place; こちら points POLITELY — at a direction ('this way'), at a place, or at a person you are introducing. こちらは せんせいです is how you present someone. Shop staff and hosts use it constantly, so you will hear it long before you need to say it.

examples.ja: こちらは せんせいです。

antiPattern.ja: これは せんせいです。
antiPattern.why: これ points at THINGS — presenting a person takes the polite こちら.
